issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is difficult to justify clinically here because the profile contains no Negative Appraisal items and the formulation marks Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other active nodes. This item introduces a strong appraisal theme that is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is not well grounded by the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items center on sensory re-experiencing, confinement/safety, and startle, but nothing suggests a vehicle-related trauma cue. For terrorism this could occur, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the other selected items and from the inactive Triggers network.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal items and no other selected items suggesting guilt, responsibility, or moral injury; for a terrorism trauma this item can occur, but here it feels clinically disconnected from the rest of the presentation.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking is a poor fit with the rest of the threat profile and trauma context. The other threat items suggest generalized hypervigilance/startle and restricted safety, but no trigger, memory, or appraisal content links the terrorism trauma to home-intrusion fear or lock-checking specifically. This makes the item feel mismatched to the formulation and selected symptoms.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items are not well supported by the rest of the profile. The cognitive formulation only links Memory with Maladaptive Strategies, so strategies should plausibly arise from intrusive trauma memory content. However, the selected strategies are heterogeneous and weakly connected to the memory and threat items provided.

issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is too specific without any corresponding trigger, memory content, or threat item tied to vehicles/transport. For a terrorism trauma this could occur, but here the rest of the profile centers on generalized hyperarousal and sensory memory rather than transport-related danger, making this item insufficiently supported and cross-node inconsistent.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The other endorsed items center on sensory trauma memories and current threat/hypervigilance after terrorism, but there are no Negative Appraisal items supporting a guilt/responsibility theme, and the formulation leaves Negative Appraisals inactive. In this profile, repeated self-blame stands out as an isolated process that is not linked to the active Memory↔Threat pattern and is therefore clinically incoherent relative to the selected items and formulation.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe a classic sensory re-experiencing / hypervigilance pattern after terrorism, but self-blame, avoiding driving, and avoiding conflict introduce themes that are not represented in the memory or threat content and therefore do not cohere well with the active Memory↔Threat formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, the selected items point in three quite different directions: moral/self-evaluative coping (self-blame), transport-specific avoidance (driving/passenger), and interpersonal avoidance (conflict). This breadth is not impossible, but here it lacks supporting trigger, appraisal, or memory content to connect them into one coherent terrorism-related syndrome.

vignette:
Kosal Phan is a 72-year-old Cambodian-American man who has spent the better part of four decades working in refugee aid, coordinating resettlement services for displaced families across the American Southeast. He came to the United States as a young man, carrying memories of upheaval he had long since learned to compartmentalise, and had built a life defined by purposeful service, a long marriage, and the quiet authority of someone who had survived much and chosen to help others survive too. That equilibrium shattered fourteen months ago when a pipe bomb detonated outside the community centre where Kosal was facilitating an intake session for newly arrived families. The blast killed two colleagues and injured eleven others. Kosal was close enough that the pressure wave knocked him from his chair. He remembers the sound before anything else - a concussive crack that seemed to compress the air out of the room - and then the images: ceiling tiles falling, a woman's shoe in the corridor, the particular quality of light through smoke-filled windows. He was physically unharmed, which he has never quite forgiven himself for.

In the weeks after the attack, Kosal found that the event resisted ordinary memory. The experience felt so catastrophic, so outside the register of anything his life should have contained, that he would sometimes catch himself thinking it could not really have happened to him - a man who had built his identity around bearing witness to others' suffering, not becoming its subject. This quality of unreality did not protect him. Instead, his memories arrived in fragments: sudden visual flashes of the collapsed ceiling, and, more disturbingly, the sound of the detonation replaying in his mind with a fidelity that startled him each time, as though the blast were occurring again at the edge of his hearing. These intrusive sensory memories began feeding a pattern of self-recrimination that settled into daily rumination. He had organised that session, had chosen that room, had greeted those families at the door. The loop of self-blame became relentless - he would lie awake reconstructing the morning's decisions, certain that a different choice would have changed everything. The memories, vivid and fragmentary as they were, supplied the raw material for this blame, each image a fresh indictment.

The same intrusive recall began reshaping how Kosal moved through the world. When the sounds returned in his mind, his body responded as though the threat were present: he would startle violently at a car backfiring, at a door slamming two offices away, at sounds his wife didn't even register. He became hypervigilant in public spaces, scanning exits, watching strangers' hands, unable to sit with his back to a room. He came to feel genuinely safe only at home, in the two rooms he could surveil completely - and even that safety was conditional. This state of chronic threat perception, in turn, made the memories more accessible. The alertness kept him primed, and being primed meant the images and sounds were never far below the surface, ready to surface fully at the slightest cue.

Over months, his world contracted. He stopped driving entirely - the confined space of a vehicle, the inability to exit quickly, had become intolerable - and began declining assignments that required travel. His supervisor, a woman he had mentored for years, eventually reassigned his field coordination role. He also began avoiding any situation that might generate conflict, withdrawing from team meetings, deflecting disagreements with silence, because confrontation now felt physically dangerous in a way he could not explain to colleagues. The relational cost has been significant: he is quieter with his wife, more absent, and she has told him gently that she misses him.

What finally brought Kosal to seek help was a moment at work last month when a fire drill - the alarm, the sudden movement of bodies - sent him to the floor behind his desk, hands over his head, before he understood consciously what he was doing. He sat there for a long time after the building emptied. He is most afraid, he says, that he has become someone who can no longer do the work that has given his life meaning. What he is hoping for, more quietly, is to stop hearing the sound.
